extracted.intended_audience: U.S. patent examiners and patent practitioners (attorneys/agents)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating whether patent claim language satisfies the definiteness requirement of 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (pre-AIA second paragraph) including related issues (terms of degree, antecedent basis, functional language, numeric ranges, exemplar language, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Breadth Is Not Indefiniteness
rubrics_metrics.description: A broad claim is not indefinite merely because it encompasses a wide scope of subject matter provided the scope is clearly defined; a claim is indefinite when the boundaries of the protected subject matter are not clearly delineated and the scope is unclear (e.g., more than one reasonable interpretation of what species are included).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between mere breadth and true indefiniteness. Undue breadth may be addressed under other statutes depending on reason: if claim is too broad because it does not set forth what inventor regards as the invention (evidence outside the application) use 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (pre-AIA second paragraph); if too broad for lack of support/enabling disclosure use 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (pre-AIA first paragraph); if too broad because it reads on the prior art use 35 U.S.C. 102 or 103.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning of Every Term Should Be Apparent (New Terminology)
rubrics_metrics.description: The meaning of every term used in a claim should be apparent from the prior art or from the specification and drawings at the time the application is filed; claim language may not be 'ambiguous, vague, incoherent, opaque, or otherwise unclear.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants may use new terms but must make clear and precise the terms used to define the invention so the metes and bounds can be ascertained. During examination give claims the broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the specification. If the specification states a term's meaning, use that meaning in examination. See cases (Packard; In re Morris; In re Zletz).

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance Requirement for Clarity with Limitations of Language and Science
rubrics_metrics.description: The requirement for clarity and precision must be balanced with the limitations of language and the science; the statute demands no more than the language permits in context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: New or evolving technologies may justify new terms. If claims, read in light of the specification, reasonably apprise skilled artisans of utilization and scope, and are as precise as the subject matter permits, no more is required. If language is less precise than the subject matter permits, the examiner should provide reasons for indefiniteness and suggest alternative claim language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terms Used Contrary to Ordinary Meaning Must Be Clearly Redefined
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant may act as his/her own lexicographer and use terms contrary to ordinary meanings only if the written description clearly redefines them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When there is more than one meaning for a term, the applicant must make clear which meaning is relied upon so a reasonable competitor or POSITA is put on notice. Cite Process Control Corp. v. HydReclaim; Hormone Research Foundation v. Genentech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Technical Dictionaries/Recognized Standards for Meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: It is appropriate to consult technical dictionaries to ascertain the accepted meaning of a term in the art where the meaning is unclear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare claim term meanings to technical dictionaries and recognized standards as guidance; see In re Barr and MPEP § 2111.01.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative Terminology: Terms of Degree
rubrics_metrics.description: Terms of degree (relative terminology) do not automatically render a claim indefinite; acceptability depends on whether one of ordinary skill in the art would understand what is claimed in light of the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the specification provides a standard for measuring the degree (examples, figures, guidelines), the claim is likely definite. If not, determine whether POSITA could nonetheless ascertain the scope (e.g., via examples or declarations). Applicants may overcome an indefiniteness rejection with evidence (e.g., 37 CFR 1.132 declarations). Case examples: Interval Licensing v. AOL; Hearing Components v. Shure; Enzo Biochem; Seattle Box.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference to a Variable Object May Render a Claim Indefinite
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that define elements in relation to a variable object (e.g., a user of unspecified height) may be indefinite if they fail to specify the reference standard or positional relationship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether a known and ascertainable standard is implicit; compare Miyazaki (large printer/user height) and Brummer (wheelbase vs. rider height) where claims were indefinite, versus Orthokinetics (pediatric wheelchair insertable through space between doorframe) which was definite because the limitation was as accurate as the subject matter permits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approximations — 'About' (Contextual Determination)
rubrics_metrics.description: The range encompassed by the term 'about' must be determined from context in the specification and claims; 'about' can be definite if the context allows clear infringement assessment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: W.L. Gore (stretch rate 'exceeding about 10% per second' definite because infringement assessable), Amgen (claims reciting 'at least about' invalid where nothing in spec/prosecution/prior art indicated the range). Consider related facts and prior art when deciding definiteness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approximations — 'Essentially'
rubrics_metrics.description: Terms like 'essentially' can be definite where the specification provides guidelines and examples enabling POSITA to draw a line between unavoidable impurities and essential ingredients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'silicon dioxide source that is essentially free of alkali metal' was definite in In re Marosi because of enabling guidelines; do not require numerical cutoffs where impractical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approximations — 'Similar'
rubrics_metrics.description: The word 'similar' may be indefinite when it is unclear what items are encompassed by the recitation of 'similar' apparatus or structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Ex parte Kristensen (nozzle 'or similar apparatus' indefinite); design patent with 'or similar structure' held indefinite in Ex parte Pappas. Ensure specification clarifies the intended scope if using 'similar.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Approximations — 'Substantially'
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'substantially' is broad but may be definite if the specification provides general guidelines or examples that inform POSITA what is meant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case law supports definiteness where the spec gives guidance (In re Nehrenberg; In re Mattison; Andrew Corp. v. Gabriel Electronics). Examiner should look for general guidelines or examples in the disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approximations — Use of 'Type' (e.g., 'X-type')
rubrics_metrics.description: Adding the word 'type' to an otherwise definite expression can extend scope and render it indefinite when it is unclear what 'type' is intended to convey.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Ex parte Copenhaver; Ex parte Attig ('ZSM-5-type' zeolites indefinite where dependent claims' zeolites were not within the genus). If 'type' is used, ensure the scope is made clear in the specification or claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subjective Terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Facially subjective terms (e.g., 'aesthetically pleasing', 'unobtrusive manner') can render a claim indefinite if the specification fails to provide an objective standard for measuring scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claim scope cannot depend solely on unrestrained subjective judgment. Examiner should determine if the spec supplies a standard analogous to a term of degree. Applicant may amend or provide evidence that POSITA can ascertain the meaning; however, examples in the spec may sometimes be insufficient (see Datamize; Interval Licensing).

rubrics_metrics.name: Numerical Ranges and Amounts — General
rubrics_metrics.description: Recitation of specific numerical ranges in a claim generally does not raise a definiteness issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nevertheless, analyze the context and related claim language for clarity issues (e.g., overlapping ranges, inconsistent dependent claims).

rubrics_metrics.name: Numerical Ranges — Narrow and Broader Ranges in the Same Claim
rubrics_metrics.description: A single claim that includes both a broad range and a narrower (preferred) range may be indefinite when it is unclear whether the narrower range is intended as a limitation, leading to confusion over the intended scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer placing narrower ranges in dependent claims or separate independent claims. If both appear in a single claim and the metes and bounds are unclear, reject under 35 U.S.C. 112(b). Examples of problematic language: 'temperature between 45 and 78°C, preferably between 50 and 60°C'; 'a predetermined quantity, for example, the maximum capacity.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Numerical Ranges — Open-Ended Numerical Ranges
rubrics_metrics.description: Open-ended numerical ranges (e.g., 'at least 20%') require careful analysis for definiteness in context, especially when dependent claims or compositions create apparent inconsistencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watch for dependent claim percentages that add up to 100% seeming to exclude the 'at least' component. Cases: In re Kroekel (theoretical >100% not per se indefinite); In re Kirsch (maximum without minimum not necessarily indefinite).

rubrics_metrics.name: Numerical Ranges — 'Effective Amount'
rubrics_metrics.description: The phrase 'an effective amount' may be definite or indefinite depending on whether POSITA could determine specific values from the disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test whether POSITA could determine specific values based on the written disclosure and examples. Examples: In re Halleck (definite where amount not critical and examples guide POSITA); In re Fredericksen (indefinite where function not stated and multiple effects implied). Ex parte Skuballa supports definiteness when disclosure provides guidelines and intended utilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exemplary Claim Language ('for example', 'such as')
rubrics_metrics.description: Description of examples or preferences belongs in the specification rather than the claims; if stated in claims, examples and preferences may lead to confusion over intended scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The mere use of 'such as' or 'for example' does not per se render a claim indefinite, but the examiner should analyze whether the metes and bounds are clearly set forth. Several fact-specific examples have been held indefinite (listed A–E in MPEP §2173.05(d)). Use caution and cite MPEP §2173.02 for context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lack of Antecedent Basis
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim is indefinite when it contains words or phrases whose meaning is unclear due to lack of antecedent basis (e.g., use of 'said lever' where no earlier recitation of a lever exists or ambiguous references to multiple like elements).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Antecedent problems are typically drafting oversights and should be identified and suggested for correction by the examiner. However, lack of antecedent basis does not always render a claim indefinite if POSITA can reasonably ascertain the scope (see Ex parte Porter; inherent components such as 'outer surface of said sphere' need not be separately recited).

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner Should Suggest Corrections to Antecedent Problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Antecedent problems are usually easily corrected once brought to applicant's attention; examiners should be constructive and suggest corrections so minimal effort is expended on drafting fixes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even though indefiniteness may be semantic, it is not excused simply because it could have been corrected. Cite In re Hammack.

rubrics_metrics.name: A Claim Term with No Antecedent Basis Is Not Necessarily Indefinite
rubrics_metrics.description: The absence of an explicit antecedent basis in the specification for a term or phrase used in the claim does not automatically render it indefinite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants have latitude in terminology choices so long as the terms and phrases define the invention with reasonable clarity and precision; evaluate whether POSITA can reasonably ascertain the scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preamble/Body Differences Do Not Per Se Render a Claim Indefinite
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim is not per se indefinite if the body recites additional elements which do not appear in the preamble; consider the totality of claim limitations to determine whether the claim apprises POSITA of its scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate all limitations and their interactions. Example: In re Larsen — court reversed an examiner rejection where the claim in its entirety apprised POSITA of scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference to Limitations in Another Claim
rubrics_metrics.description: Making reference to a preceding claim to define a limitation is acceptable and need not be rejected merely because of the cross-reference (e.g., 'the product produced by the method of claim 1').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such references are permissible if they do not create confusion. If the referencing format causes confusion, a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) is proper. When examining dependent claims, also assess compliance with 35 U.S.C. 112(d) (pre-AIA fourth paragraph) and MPEP §608.01(n).

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional Limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim term is functional when it recites a feature by what it does rather than by what it is; functional language is not inherently improper and is often permissible (including non-means-plus-function forms).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate functional limitations by what they fairly convey to POSITA in context. Means-plus-function claiming under 35 U.S.C. 112(f) (pre-AIA sixth paragraph) applies only to purely functional limitations lacking structure; otherwise functional language is interpreted with full ordinary meaning absent clear disavowal. Examples/cases: In re Swinehart; In re Schreiber; Innova/Pure Water v. Safari; In re Barr; In re Venezia. Ensure that the claim provides sufficient disclosure where required or use 112(f) analysis (see MPEP §2181).
